will be educated, how data will be managed, how decisions will be made 
about selecting and implementing new technologies and how continuous 
improvement will be approached.
RECOMMENDATION 2
Education  
It is recommended that schools routinely 
provide education about the responsible use 
of performance technologies to those involved 
with their use. Education is foundational for 
informed consent, and it aids in ensuring 
schools use performance technologies in a 
way that maximizes benefits and minimizes 
harm to student-athletes. 
Strategy 2.1
At least once annually, provide education to those involved in 
selecting, using or accessing data from performance technologies.
Strategy 2.2
Educational needs are likely to vary among different groups 
and schools should consider tailoring education to meet 
each group’s learning needs. Such groups may include,  
but are not limited to, student-athletes, coaches, strength 
and conditioning staff, sports medicine staff  
and administration.
Strategy 2.3
Address topics such as:
• Limitations and potential harms of  
performance technologies.
• Data privacy and security.
• Student-athlete rights and protections  
(e.g., informed consent).
• Departmental policies and procedures  
for responsible use.


=== PAGE 4 ===
4
RECOMMENDATION 3
Data Management  
It is recommended that schools establish 
who owns data from performance 
technologies, where and how data is 
stored, who has the authority to access 
data and how data is permitted to be used. 
Performance technologies have different 
use-case scenarios and produce different 
types of data, and the interpretation and 
communication of data may benefit from 
a multidisciplinary approach. Schools may 
consider using existing campus resources for 
data management in collaboration with legal 
and risk management personnel. 
Strategy 3.1 
Determine who can be involved in interpreting and sharing/communicating 
data from performance technologies, including considerations for the required 
competencies and oversight necessary to do so effectively and responsibly. 
Strategy 3.2
Determine what rights, if any, the school has with respect to data collection, 
data use, data access and ownership of the performance technology data, 
including considerations for transfer student-athletes.
Strategy 3.3
Clarify the school’s permissible uses of data from performance technologies. 
If data might be used to inform medical decision-making, sports medicine staff 
should be involved. Schools should refer to independent medical care best 
practices to ensure the unchallengeable, autonomous authority of primary 
athletics healthcare providers to determine medical management and return-
to-play decisions of student-athletes.
RECOMMENDATION 4
Selecting and 
Implementing New 
Technologies  
It is recommended that schools establish a 
structured process for making decisions about 
selecting and implementing new performance 
technologies. A structured process 
that considers how to use performance 
technologies in a way that maximizes benefits 
and minimizes harm is important to ensure 
student-athlete well-being is prioritized when 
a school makes decisions regarding use of 
performance technologies.
Strategy 4.1
Review technologies using existing, evidence-based standards and 
frameworks that evaluate their value, usability and quality.
Strategy 4.2
Consider and assess the quality of performance technologies. Quality may 
include, but is not limited to, factors such as accuracy, reliability, validity 
and function.
Strategy 4.3
Decisions about selecting and implementing performance technologies 
should be made by a multidisciplinary group. Important roles to consider 
including are sports medicine staff and individuals with competencies 
in sports science, coaching staff, information technology, data security, 
administration and compliance.


=== PAGE 5 ===
5
NCAA is a trademark of the National Collegiate Athletic Association. March 2026.
RECOMMENDATION 5
Continuous 
Improvement  
It is recommended that schools routinely 
get feedback from those using performance 
technologies (e.g., student-athletes, coaches, 
sports medicine staff) about how these 
technologies are being used and how they 
are working. This feedback can be used to 
inform changes to the school’s written plan to 
reflect current needs, available resources and 
evolving technological developments.
Strategy 5.1
Engage a multidisciplinary group to plan, collect and interpret feedback about 
performance technologies. When possible, this group should include individuals 
involved in establishing the school’s written plan for responsible use.
Strategy 5.2
Understanding student-athletes’ experiences with performance technology 
is critical. Schools should obtain student-athlete feedback to learn about the 
positive and/or negative impacts performance technology use has on their 
student-athletes.
Strategy 5.3
Areas for feedback from additional groups could include:
• Technology implementation (e.g., how were technologies used).
• Technology effectiveness (e.g., how did outcomes align with the school’s 
reasons for their use).
• Education (e.g., does education meet learner needs).
Additional guidance 
and resources related to 
training and performance 
topics can be found by 
scanning the QR code above.
Performance technologies are just one tool schools 
might consider using to address student-athlete 
health, safety and performance.

3	[Normal] The responsible use of performance technology in collegiate athletics requires balancing innovation with safeguarding student-athlete health and well-being.

5	[Normal] The NCAA Committee developed recommendations to help schools innovate while protecting athletes. 
6	[Normal] Key areas include thoughtful policy setting, ongoing education, secure data handling, and continuous review. 
7	[Normal] The goal is to ensure technologies enhance performance without compromising safety or mental health. 
8	[Normal] Tim Coffey and Mark Coberly contributed directly to crafting these guidelines.
9	[Normal] Technology Must Be Used as a Tool, Not a Solution
10	[Normal] Tim highlighted that technologies like wearables and sensors provide data but don’t solve problems alone. 
11	[Normal] Mark emphasized asking specific questions before selecting tools to avoid data overload. 
12	[Normal] Both agreed that data should guide decisions but not dictate them blindly, respecting individual contexts. 
13	[Normal] This mindset helps avoid misuse and supports targeted care and performance improvements.
14	[Normal] Written Plans Are Essential to Manage Technology Use and Avoid Risks
15	[Normal] Mark described developing policies that require purchasers to justify technology with clear questions. 
16	[Normal] Plans must address data validity, reliability, usage protocols, data ownership, and access controls. 
17	[Normal] Regular reevaluation is critical to assess ongoing value, actionable insights, and unintended consequences. 
18	[Normal] This structured approach prevents impulse buys driven by peer pressure or hype.
19	[Normal] Risks Include Misuse of Data and Mental Health Impacts
20	[Normal] Mark warned about dangers of ignoring critical data or misinterpreting it, which can harm athletes and institutions. 
21	[Normal] Tim shared research showing data surveillance can cause anxiety and fear among athletes. 
22	[Normal] Misuse risks increase without clear policies on access, interpretation, and communication. 
23	[Normal] Proactive, transparent education and consent processes help mitigate these risks.
24	[Normal] Types and Evolution of Performance Technologies
25	[Normal] Performance technologies span wearable devices, equipment sensors, optical systems, lab-grade tools, and personal surveys, and they keep evolving in use and complexity.
26	[Normal] Diverse Tools Capture Physical and Personal Metrics
27	[Normal] Tim described wearables like heart rate monitors and sweat lactate patches worn by athletes. 
28	[Normal] Equipment-based tools include tags on bats measuring swing speed. 
29	[Normal] Optical camera systems track athlete positions and motion metrics on the field. 
30	[Normal] Lab-grade devices such as DEXA scanners and force plates assess body composition and biomechanics. 
31	[Normal] Personal surveys track mood, sleep, and menstrual cycles, integrating subjective athlete data.
32	[Normal] Use Cases Depend on Team Culture and Implementation
33	[Normal] Tim shared examples where a scale was used differently across teams, either as a hydration guide or avoided due to body image concerns. 
34	[Normal] This illustrates the importance of adapting technology use to athlete needs and cultural context. 
35	[Normal] Coaches and trainers need to understand the technology’s role rather than blindly applying metrics. 
36	[Normal] Proper use respects psychological safety and enhances meaningful insights.
37	[Normal] Increasing Access to Advanced Tools Raises New Opportunities and Challenges
38	[Normal] More programs now use lab-grade equipment previously limited to elite settings. 
39	[Normal] This allows deeper physical profiling but requires careful interpretation and integration. 
40	[Normal] Awareness of how these tools fit into broader athlete management is growing. 
41	[Normal] Education on data validity is essential as usage spreads.
42	[Normal] Self-Report Data Is Often Overlooked but Critical
43	[Normal] Surveys and mood tracking capture important personal experiences often missed by physical sensors. 
44	[Normal] These data feed into athlete management systems alongside objective measures. 
45	[Normal] Recognizing their value helps create a fuller picture of athlete health and readiness. 
46	[Normal] They require sensitive handling due to privacy concerns.
47	[Normal] Data Ownership, Privacy, and Security
48	[Normal] Managing athlete data demands clear policies on ownership, storage, privacy, and access to protect sensitive information.
49	[Normal] Legal Complexity Surrounds Data Protection and Privacy
50	[Normal] Tim emphasized consulting general counsel because state laws vary and HIPAA coverage is unclear. 
51	[Normal] Physiological data like heart rate is more likely HIPAA-protected than performance metrics like sprint times. 
52	[Normal] Many campuses underestimate the sensitivity of collected data and risks of sharing or publicizing it. 
53	[Normal] De-identification often fails to fully anonymize athletes, posing re-identification risks.
54	[Normal] Data Storage and Access Must Meet Institutional Security Standards
55	[Normal] Universities must control where data is stored, who can access it, and how securely it is handled. 
56	[Normal] Cloud storage raises concerns given past incidents with educational platforms. 
57	[Normal] Collaboration with IT and risk management departments is crucial for safe data governance. 
58	[Normal] Contracts with vendors should be reviewed carefully to understand data resale or secondary use terms.
59	[Normal] Transparency with Student Athletes About Data Use and Consent Is Essential
60	[Normal] Mark stressed the need to educate athletes on what data is collected and who sees it. 
61	[Normal] Athletes should be able to opt out of wearable or survey data collection where feasible. 
62	[Normal] Some data, like video tracking, may be unavoidable but still requires clear communication. 
63	[Normal] This transparency builds trust and reduces anxiety around data surveillance.
64	[Normal] Vendor Practices Can Complicate Data Ownership 
65	[Normal] Some companies offer discounts in exchange for selling collected data, which they may not fully disclose internally. 
66	[Normal] Purchasing decision-makers must understand these implications for athlete privacy and institutional reputation. 
67	[Normal] Vendors must be transparent about how they use de-identified data for research or norm-building. 
68	[Normal] Legal and IT teams should closely vet contracts.
69	[Normal] Education and Stakeholder Engagement
70	[Normal] Education for all stakeholders is vital to ensure proper use, interpretation, and consent regarding performance technologies.
71	[Normal] Performance and Sports Medicine Staff Require Deep Training
72	[Normal] Mark highlighted that coaches, trainers, and performance staff must understand technology validity and what the data mean. 
73	[Normal] Misinterpreting metrics can lead to poor decisions and erode athlete trust. 
74	[Normal] Staff should agree on data use policies and interpretation standards before applying technology. 
75	[Normal] Ongoing education helps keep pace with evolving tools.
76	[Normal] Coaches Need Awareness Without Overload
77	[Normal] Coaches should understand what data impacts their decisions and how technology informs practice or recovery. 
78	[Normal] This knowledge supports buy-in and practical adjustments rather than ignoring collected data. 
79	[Normal] Tailored education prevents confusion and resistance. 
80	[Normal] Coaches’ feedback on data utility is important for refining technology use.
81	[Normal] Student Athletes Must Be Informed and Consent to Data Collection
82	[Normal] Athletes should know what technologies are used, how data is handled, and their rights about participation. 
83	[Normal] Education reduces anxiety and improves cooperation. 
84	[Normal] Consent processes are often missing and need strengthening. 
85	[Normal] Listening to athlete feedback about technology impact is critical.
86	[Normal] Feedback Loops Should Involve Athletes, Coaches, and Medical Staff
87	[Normal] Tim recommended collecting feedback regularly through surveys and direct conversations. 
88	[Normal] This helps assess technology effectiveness, acceptance, and any unintended effects. 
89	[Normal] Feedback supports adaptive management and continuous improvement. 
90	[Normal] Rapid roster changes due to transfers make ongoing communication essential.
91	[Normal] Misconceptions and Challenges in Technology Use
92	[Normal] Understanding limitations, variability, and the “black box” nature of some performance metrics is key to realistic expectations.
93	[Normal] No Single Metric Predicts Performance or Risk Reliably 
94	[Normal] Tim pointed out human performance varies widely, making single-number assessments misleading. 
95	[Normal] Technology claims often oversimplify complex physiology and biomechanics. 
96	[Normal] Decisions should be based on trends and multiple data points, not isolated scores. 
97	[Normal] Overreliance on imperfect metrics can misguide training or medical decisions.
98	[Normal] Black Box Algorithms Obscure How Numbers Are Calculated
99	[Normal] Both Tim and Mark noted many vendors do not disclose formulas behind key performance scores. 
100	[Normal] Conflicting results from competing devices complicate clinical or coaching decisions. 
101	[Normal] Lack of transparency undermines trust and scientific validity. 
102	[Normal] Clinicians emphasize the need for validated reliable tools before medical decisions.
103	[Normal] Mental Health Impacts of Data Surveillance Are Real and Often Overlooked
104	[Normal] Studies in professional rugby revealed anxiety caused by opaque monitoring and grading systems. 
105	[Normal] Similar effects appear in collegiate athletes, especially with leaderboards or public displays. 
106	[Normal] Awareness and education can reduce negative psychological consequences. 
107	[Normal] Policies should consider the mental health dimension as part of responsible technology use.
108	[Normal] Technologies Must Be Regularly Evaluated for Continued Value
109	[Normal] Mark stressed the importance of assessing whether investments lead to actionable insights. 
110	[Normal] If data does not change decisions or improve outcomes, the technology should be reconsidered. 
111	[Normal] This evaluation prevents waste and supports a value-driven approach. 
112	[Normal] Continuous learning and adaptation are necessary in a rapidly evolving field.
113	[Normal] Strategic Integration and Future Directions
114	[Normal] Integrating performance technologies with medical records and fostering data-guided decisions will improve athlete outcomes and competitive success.
115	[Normal] Combining Medical Records with Performance Data Offers Injury Mitigation Opportunities
116	[Normal] Mark described emerging efforts to link health records with technology data for injury risk trends. 
117	[Normal] This integration requires cross-department education and coach buy-in. 
118	[Normal] Successful adoption can lead to healthier teams and better performance. 
119	[Normal] High-performing programs are moving toward this holistic data approach.
120	[Normal] A Values-Driven Approach Focuses on Return on Investment and Purpose
121	[Normal] Mark defined value as whether technology investments answer key questions and impact decisions. 
122	[Normal] Regular reviews of utility and impact help ensure resources are well spent. 
123	[Normal] This approach discourages fads and encourages strategic adoption. 
124	[Normal] It aligns technology use with institutional goals and athlete welfare.
125	[Normal] Ongoing Learning and Adaptation Are Critical in This Rapidly Changing Field 
126	[Normal] Tim stressed that no one has all the answers given the novelty and speed of technology advances. 
127	[Normal] The NCAA recommendations provide a solid foundation but must evolve with new insights. 
128	[Normal] Awareness of potential side effects and unintended consequences remains vital. 
129	[Normal] Continuous collaboration among researchers, clinicians, coaches, and athletes drives progress.
130	[Normal] Multidisciplinary Collaboration Enhances Policy and Practice Development
131	[Normal] Involving legal, IT, risk management, medical, and coaching staff ensures comprehensive oversight. 
132	[Normal] This team approach helps balance innovation with privacy, safety, and ethical concerns. 
133	[Normal] It supports clear communication and accountability around data use. 
134	[Normal] Collaborative frameworks enable sustainable and responsible technology integration.
135	[Normal] KEY TAKEAWAYS OVERVIEW
136	[Normal] Responsible Technology Use: Balance innovation with athlete health; set policies, educate, secure data, and regularly review technology impact.
137	[Normal] Technology as a Tool: Use wearables and sensors to guide decisions, not replace context-aware judgment; avoid data overload and misuse.
138	[Normal] Data Privacy and Security: Consult legal teams on data laws; ensure secure storage and clear athlete consent; watch for vendor data selling.
139	[Normal] Stakeholder Education: Train staff deeply on data meaning; keep coaches informed without overwhelming; fully educate athletes and obtain consent.
140	[Normal] Technology Limitations: No single metric reliably predicts performance; be wary of opaque algorithms; consider mental health effects of data use.
141	[Normal] Strategic Integration: Link medical and performance data for injury prevention; continuously evaluate tech value and foster multidisciplinary collaboration.

## Summary

### Overview

- **Responsible Technology Use:** Balance innovation with athlete health; set policies, educate, secure data, and regularly review technology impact.

- **Technology as a Tool:** Use wearables and sensors to guide decisions, not replace context-aware judgment; avoid data overload and misuse.

- **Data Privacy and Security:** Consult legal teams on data laws; ensure secure storage and clear athlete consent; watch for vendor data selling.

- **Stakeholder Education:** Train staff deeply on data meaning; keep coaches informed without overwhelming; fully educate athletes and obtain consent.

- **Technology Limitations:** No single metric reliably predicts performance; be wary of opaque algorithms; consider mental health effects of data use.

- **Strategic Integration:** Link medical and performance data for injury prevention; continuously evaluate tech value and foster multidisciplinary collaboration.

entries.name: mcp__claude_ai_Fireflies__fireflies_get_transcript
entries.description: Fetches detailed meeting transcript by ID, with optional field filtering. Returns transcript content (sentences, speakers) and metadata, but excludes summary data. Each sentence is prefixed with its timestamp range (e.g. "[00:05 - 00:08] Speaker: text") so moments can be anchored back to the recording. To link a user directly to a moment in the meeting, convert the sentence start timestamp to seconds and build a deep link: https://app.fireflies.ai/view/{transcriptId}?t={seconds} (e.g. ?t=441.29 for 07:21). If you need summary data, use fireflies_get_summary instead. If the meeting is currently live (is_live: true), the transcript returned is a point-in-time snapshot of the live transcript with sentences captured so far.

entries.name: mcp__claude_ai_Fireflies__fireflies_get_transcripts
entries.description: Queries multiple meeting transcripts using filter properties (date, keyword, email, etc.). Returns basic metadata and transcript summary. Does NOT accept transcriptId as input - use fireflies_get_transcript() multiple times to get detailed transcript content. Each result includes the meeting id, which can be linked as https://app.fireflies.ai/view/{id}; append ?t={seconds} (e.g. ?t=441.29) to deep-link to a specific moment in the recording.

keyword.description: Optional keyword to search for in meeting content

scope.description: Optional scope for keyword search: "title" (meeting titles only), "sentences" (transcript content), or "all" (both)

fromDate.description: Optional ISO 8601 date string (e.g., "2023-01-01") to filter meetings from this date

toDate.description: Optional ISO 8601 date string (e.g., "2023-12-31") to filter meetings until this date

limit.description: Optional limit for the number of meetings to return (max 50)

skip.description: Optional number of meetings to skip for pagination

organizers.description: Optional array of organizer email addresses to filter meetings (max 50)

participants.description: Optional array of participant email addresses to filter meetings (max 50)

mine.description: Optional filter to only include meetings owned by the authenticated user

channelId.description: Optional channel/folder ID to only include meetings in that channel. Use fireflies_list_channels() to find channel IDs.

format.description: Optional response format: "toon" (default, token-efficient), "json" (standard JSON), or "text" (human-readable)

entries.name: mcp__claude_ai_Fireflies__fireflies_search
entries.description:
Advanced search for meeting transcripts using a mini grammar. Supports complex queries with multiple filters.

GRAMMAR SYNTAX:
- keyword:"search term" - Search for keywords in the content. If no scope is specified, the default scope is 'all'.
- scope:title|sentences|all - Define the search scope. Options are 'title', 'sentences', or 'all'. The default is 'all'.
- from:YYYY-MM-DD - Filter meetings from this date (ISO format)
- to:YYYY-MM-DD - Filter meetings until this date (ISO format)
- limit:N - Limit results (max 50)
- skip:N - Skip N results for pagination
- organizers:email1@x.com,email2@x.com - Filter by organizer emails (comma-separated)
- participants:email1@x.com,email2@x.com - Filter by participant emails (comma-separated)
- mine:true|false - Filter to only include user's own meetings
- channel:CHANNEL_ID - Filter meetings by channel/folder ID (use fireflies_list_channels() to find channel IDs)

EXAMPLES:
- "engineering standup" (simple keyword search)
- "keyword:\"performance\" scope:sentences limit:20"
- "channel:64f1a2b3c4d5e6f7a8b9c0d1 from:2026-01-01 limit:20"

query.description: Search query using the mini grammar syntax. Can be simple keywords or complex filters using the grammar.

format.description: Optional response format: "toon" (default, token-efficient), "json" (standard JSON), or "text" (human-readable)

You may decline to participate or withdraw consent at any time without penalty or impact on your athletic scholarship, playing time, or standing on the team. You have the right to: view your own data, ask questions about how it is used, and request corrections or deletion (subject to legal retention requirements).

327	Informing return-to-play decisions (sports medicine only) | Using body composition data to restrict access to meals or dining
328	Evaluating effectiveness of training programs | Making scholarship or roster decisions based solely on technology data

333	What the NCAA Says:
334	It is recommended that schools establish a structured process for making decisions about selecting and implementing new performance technologies. A structured process that considers how to use performance technologies in a way that maximizes benefits and minimizes harm is important to ensure student-athlete well-being is prioritized.

336	NCAA Strategy: Review technologies using existing, evidence-based standards and frameworks that evaluate their value, usability, and quality.

338	Evaluation Criteria | Questions to Answer | Score (1-5)
339	1. Scientific Validity | Is there peer-reviewed research supporting the technology's claims? Has it been validated in collegiate or athletic populations? Are the vendor's claims backed by independent evidence? | [  ]
340	2. Accuracy | Does the device measure what it claims to measure? What is the margin of error? Has accuracy been tested across different conditions (e.g., different sports, environments)? | [  ]
341	3. Reliability | Does the device produce consistent results under the same conditions? What is the test-retest reliability? | [  ]
342	4. Data Security | Where is data stored? Is it encrypted? Who has access? What is the vendor's breach notification policy? Is the vendor compliant with relevant regulations? | [  ]
343	5. Data Portability | Can data be exported in standard formats? What happens to data if we discontinue the platform? | [  ]
344	6. Usability | How easy is it to use for staff and student-athletes? What training is required? Is the user interface intuitive? | [  ]
345	7. Integration | Does it integrate with our existing systems? Are there compatibility issues with other technologies we use? | [  ]
346	8. Cost-Benefit | What is the total cost (purchase, subscription, maintenance, training)? Does the expected value justify the expense? What is the expected ROI? | [  ]
347	9. Fit with Program Needs | Does this technology solve an actual problem we have? Or is it a solution looking for a problem? Is there a cheaper or simpler alternative? | [  ]
348	10. Student-Athlete Impact | Could this technology have unintended negative effects on student-athlete well-being? Does it require significant time or effort from student-athletes? | [  ]

file.content:
[Normal] NCAA Performance Technologies
[Normal] Recommendations
[Normal] Comprehensive Action Plan for Baylor Athletics
[Normal] Prepared by Coach Rash
[Normal] Baylor University Department of Athletics
[Normal] March 2026
[Normal] WORKING DOCUMENT
[Normal] For internal use. Subject to revision based on stakeholder input.
[Heading 1] Table of Contents
[Heading 1] Introduction
[Normal] In March 2026, the NCAA Sport Science Institute published Performance Technologies Recommendations: Responsible Use in Collegiate Athletics, a consensus document developed from the May 2025 NCAA Summit on Performance Technologies. The document provides member schools with a framework for responsibly using performance technologies, organized around five core recommendations: Policy, Education, Data Management, Technology Selection, and Continuous Improvement.
[Normal] This action plan translates those recommendations into a detailed, Baylor-specific implementation roadmap. Each section includes the NCAA language, what it means for our department, specific action items with assigned deliverables, and draft templates or sample language that the working group can adapt as we move forward.
[Normal] Baylor Athletics does not currently have formal performance technology policies in place. This plan is designed to build the foundation from scratch, leveraging existing structures (annual compliance sessions, SAAC, campus IT, and legal resources) wherever possible.
[Heading 2] How to Use This Document
[Normal] Each recommendation section follows a consistent structure:
[List Paragraph] Blue callout box: The NCAA recommendation language, quoted directly.
[List Paragraph] Gold callout box: The specific NCAA strategy statement being addressed.
[List Paragraph] "What This Means for Baylor": Plain-language interpretation of how this applies to us.
[List Paragraph] Key Actions: Checkbox items for the working group to track.
[List Paragraph] Deliverable: The specific output expected from each action area.
[List Paragraph] Draft Templates: Sample language, forms, or frameworks ready for adaptation.
[Heading 1] Recommendation 1: Policy
[Heading 2] What This Means for Baylor
[Normal] We need a formal, written policy document that serves as the governing framework for how Baylor Athletics uses performance technologies. This is not a one-time exercise. The NCAA expects it to be developed by a cross-functional team, reviewed regularly, and updated as technologies and needs evolve. Every other recommendation in this document (education, data management, purchasing, and feedback) ties back to this written plan.
[Heading 2] Strategy 1.1: Assemble a Multidisciplinary Working Group
[Normal] Key Actions:
[List Paragraph] Identify a chair/lead for the working group. This person should have the organizational authority to coordinate across departments and the bandwidth to drive the process forward. Recommended candidates: Associate AD for Student-Athlete Services, Director of Sports Medicine, or a senior administrator with cross-departmental oversight.
[List Paragraph] Recruit representatives from each required area. The NCAA specifically names the following roles. Each representative should have decision-making authority or direct access to decision-makers in their area:
[List Paragraph] Student-Athletes: Minimum two representatives, ideally from different sports and genders. SAAC members or sport captains are strong candidates. Their voice is not advisory; it is essential.
[List Paragraph] Sports Medicine/Athletic Training: Head athletic trainer or designee. This person will be critical for data management (Rec 3) and ensuring the independent medical authority is protected.
[List Paragraph] Strength and Conditioning: Director of S&C or senior staff member. S&C is typically the primary operator of wearable technologies and force plates.
[List Paragraph] Coaching: Minimum two sport representatives from different sports. Coaches are end-users of performance data and need a seat at the table.
[List Paragraph] Athletics Administration: Associate AD or senior administrator who can approve policy and allocate resources.
[List Paragraph] Legal Affairs/Compliance: University legal counsel or athletics compliance officer. Essential for data privacy, consent, and regulatory considerations.
[List Paragraph] Information Technology: Campus IT or athletics IT representative. Responsible for data security, storage, vendor integration, and breach response.
[List Paragraph] Define the group charter. The working group should have a clear written charter that includes:
[List Paragraph] Mission: Develop, maintain, and oversee Baylor Athletics' written plan for the responsible use of performance technologies.
[List Paragraph] Scope: All performance technologies used across Baylor Athletics, including devices, software, apps, and surveys that collect biometric or performance data.
[List Paragraph] Responsibilities: Draft and maintain the written plan, review and approve new technology purchases, oversee education programs, collect and act on feedback, and ensure compliance with applicable laws.
[List Paragraph] Meeting cadence: Monthly during initial development (March through June 2026), then quarterly once the plan is established.
[List Paragraph] Decision-making: Consensus-based where possible; chair breaks ties. Legal has veto authority on compliance matters.
[List Paragraph] Set the initial meeting schedule. Book monthly meetings through June 2026. The first meeting should focus on reviewing this document and the NCAA source material, and on assigning ownership of plan sections.
[Normal] Deliverable:
[Normal] Working Group Charter Document (1-2 pages) documenting mission, membership, roles, meeting cadence, and decision-making process.
[Normal] Draft Template: Working Group Charter
[Heading 2] Strategy 1.2: Draft the Written Plan
[Normal] The written plan is the central deliverable. It should be a single, comprehensive document (or a policy manual with clearly organized sections) that anyone in the department can reference. Below is the recommended structure and the content each section should address.
[Normal] Key Actions:
[List Paragraph] Create a policy document organized around the following sections:
[List Paragraph] Route the draft through legal affairs and compliance for review. Legal should review for: applicable privacy laws (FERPA, Texas data privacy, any biometric privacy considerations), adequacy of informed consent language, data breach notification obligations, and alignment with university-wide policies.
[List Paragraph] Establish version control. Use a naming convention (e.g., BaylorAthletics_PerfTech_Policy_v1.0_2026-06) and maintain a revision log on the first page of the document. Store the master copy in a central location accessible to all working group members.
[List Paragraph] Set an annual review date. The plan should be reviewed at least annually. Recommend tying the review to the start of each academic year (August/September) so updates can be communicated during preseason meetings.
[Normal] Deliverable:
[Normal] Baylor Athletics Performance Technology Policy (estimated 15-25 pages with appendices). Target completion: June 2026.
[Heading 1] Recommendation 2: Education
[Heading 2] What This Means for Baylor
[Normal] Everyone who touches performance technology needs training, and that training needs to happen at least once a year. The good news: Baylor already has annual compliance and onboarding sessions. We can build performance technology modules into those existing structures rather than creating an entirely new training apparatus. The key is tailoring the content to different audiences, because a student-athlete and a compliance officer need very different information.
[Heading 2] Strategy 2.1: Provide Annual Education to All Involved
[Normal] Key Actions:
[List Paragraph] Map every person/role that interacts with performance technology. Create a comprehensive list of who selects, operates, interprets, accesses, or makes decisions based on performance technology data. This becomes your required-training roster.
[List Paragraph] Integrate performance technology training into existing annual sessions:
[List Paragraph] Staff annual compliance meeting: Add a 30-45 minute performance technology module covering policy overview, data handling responsibilities, and any updates from the previous year.
[List Paragraph] New student-athlete orientation: Add a 20-30 minute segment on performance technology rights, informed consent, what data is collected, and how to raise concerns.
[List Paragraph] Returning student-athlete preseason meeting: Add a brief (10-15 minute) refresher covering any new technologies introduced, policy changes, or updated consent requirements.
[List Paragraph] New hire onboarding: Include performance technology policy review for any new coaches, S&C staff, athletic trainers, or administrators.
[List Paragraph] Create an attendance tracking system. Use sign-in sheets or digital tracking (LMS if available) to document who completed training and when. This is your compliance record if questions arise.
[List Paragraph] Store all training materials centrally. Maintain a shared folder (e.g., on the athletics shared drive or LMS) with all slide decks, handouts, and reference materials so staff can review them at any time.
[Normal] Deliverable:
[Normal] An annual education calendar that maps each audience to their training session, timing, and delivery method.
[Normal] Draft Template: Annual Education Calendar
[Heading 2] Strategy 2.2: Tailor Education by Audience
[Normal] A one-size-fits-all presentation will not work. Below is a detailed breakdown of what each audience needs to know, along with sample talking points and curriculum outlines.
[Normal] Key Actions:
[List Paragraph] Develop a Student-Athlete Education Module covering:
[List Paragraph] What performance technologies are and why Baylor uses them.
[List Paragraph] Exactly what data is collected about them (types, frequency, devices).
[List Paragraph] Who can see their data and who cannot (access controls by role).
[List Paragraph] How their data is stored, how long it is kept, and what happens when they graduate or transfer.
[List Paragraph] Their right to informed consent: what they are agreeing to, that participation is voluntary, how to withdraw, and that declining will not affect their standing on the team.
[List Paragraph] Potential negative effects to watch for (data fixation, anxiety about metrics, body image concerns from body composition tracking) and who to talk to if they experience them.
[List Paragraph] How to raise concerns or file a complaint about how their data is being used.
[Normal] Draft Template: Sample Student-Athlete Talking Points
[List Paragraph] Develop a Coaches Education Module covering:
[List Paragraph] Overview of available performance technologies and what data they produce.
[List Paragraph] What data coaches are permitted to access and what is restricted (e.g., medical data, mental health screening results).
[List Paragraph] Limitations of performance technology data: these are tools, not crystal balls. Data should supplement coaching judgment, not replace it.
[List Paragraph] Responsible communication about data with student-athletes (avoid using data punitively or publicly).
[List Paragraph] The boundary between coaching decisions and medical decisions: sports medicine retains independent, unchallengeable authority over medical management and return-to-play.
[List Paragraph] Departmental policies and the consequences of policy violations.
[List Paragraph] Develop modules for S&C Staff, Sports Medicine, and Administration. Each should be tailored to their specific responsibilities as outlined in the audience focus table below:
[Heading 2] Strategy 2.3: Address Required Topics
[Normal] The NCAA names four specific topic areas. All four should appear in every audience module, though the depth and emphasis will vary. Below is a more detailed breakdown of what each topic should cover.
[Normal] Deliverable:
[Normal] Five audience-specific training modules (slide decks and/or handouts) covering all four required topics, tailored to each group. Target completion: June 2026 for initial versions; reviewed and updated annually.
[Heading 1] Recommendation 3: Data Management
[Heading 2] What This Means for Baylor
[Normal] This is the most complex recommendation because it sits at the intersection of legal, IT, sports medicine, and coaching. We need clear, documented answers to four questions: Who owns the data? Where does it live? Who can see it? What can it be used for? We also need specific protocols for transfer student-athletes and for situations where data informs medical decisions.
[Heading 2] Strategy 3.1: Define Who Interprets and Shares Data
[Normal] Key Actions:
[List Paragraph] Create a Data Touchpoint Map. For every performance technology currently in use (identified during the technology inventory), document: what data it produces, who collects it, who interprets it, who it is shared with, and where it is stored.
[Normal] Draft Template: Data Touchpoint Map
[List Paragraph] Define competency requirements for data interpretation. Not everyone should be interpreting every type of data. Establish minimum qualifications:
[List Paragraph] Health-related data (HRV, wellness, body composition): Interpretation restricted to sports medicine staff, licensed athletic trainers, or individuals with documented sports science credentials.
[List Paragraph] Training load and performance data (GPS, force plates, velocity): Interpretation by certified S&C professionals or individuals with sports science competencies.
[List Paragraph] Aggregate/summary data (team averages, trends): May be shared with coaches and administration in summarized form, with context provided by the interpreting professional.
[List Paragraph] Establish data sharing rules. Create a clear matrix showing who can share what with whom:
[List Paragraph] Assign a Data Steward. Designate one person responsible for overseeing compliance with data policies, managing access requests, and serving as the point of contact for data-related questions. Recommended: someone in sports medicine or athletics administration with IT coordination.
[Normal] Deliverable:
[Normal] Data Touchpoint Map and Data Access Matrix documents. Target: April 2026 (draft), May 2026 (finalized with legal review).
[Heading 2] Strategy 3.2: Clarify Data Ownership and Rights
[Normal] Key Actions:
[List Paragraph] Conduct a vendor contract audit. For every technology platform in use, pull the contract/terms of service and identify:
[List Paragraph] Who owns the data: Baylor, the student-athlete, or the vendor?
[List Paragraph] Where data is stored: On-premise, vendor cloud, third-party servers? In what jurisdiction?
[List Paragraph] Data retention: How long does the vendor keep data? Can we request deletion?
[List Paragraph] Data portability: Can we export our data if we switch vendors? In what format?
[List Paragraph] Breach notification: What is the vendor obligated to do if there is a data breach?
[List Paragraph] Work with legal to establish Baylor's position on data ownership. The recommendation is that Baylor assert ownership of all performance technology data collected from its student-athletes, with the student-athlete retaining the right to access their own data.
[List Paragraph] Develop a Transfer Student-Athlete Data Protocol:
[List Paragraph] Outgoing transfers: Student-athlete may request a copy of their data. Baylor retains its copy for [defined retention period]. Data is not proactively sent to the new school without the student-athlete's written request.
[List Paragraph] Incoming transfers: Baylor does not request performance technology data from the previous school. If the student-athlete voluntarily provides data, it is reviewed by sports medicine before being incorporated into Baylor systems.
[List Paragraph] Data deletion: Student-athletes may request deletion of their data upon departure, subject to any legal retention requirements.
[List Paragraph] Build data rights into the informed consent form. The consent form (see template below) should clearly state: what data is collected, how it will be used, who will access it, how long it will be retained, what happens at graduation/transfer, and how to withdraw consent.
[Normal] Draft Template: Draft Informed Consent Form (Key Sections)
[Normal] Deliverable:
[Normal] Informed Consent Form Template (reviewed and approved by legal). Transfer Student-Athlete Data Protocol (1-2 pages). Vendor Contract Audit Summary (spreadsheet). Target: May 2026.
[Heading 2] Strategy 3.3: Establish Permissible Uses of Data
[Normal] Key Actions:
[List Paragraph] Create an Approved Uses / Prohibited Uses list:
[List Paragraph] Codify independent medical authority. Include explicit language in the written plan stating that sports medicine staff retain final, unchallengeable authority over all medical management and return-to-play decisions, regardless of what performance technology data may suggest. Coaches and administrators may not override medical judgment based on data. Reference the NCAA Independent Medical Care Best Practices.
[List Paragraph] Coordinate with IT on data security. Work with IT to ensure:
[List Paragraph] All performance technology data is stored on encrypted systems.
[List Paragraph] Access is controlled through role-based permissions (matching the Data Access Matrix).
[List Paragraph] Backup and disaster recovery procedures are in place.
[List Paragraph] A data breach response plan exists and is tested.
[Normal] Deliverable:
[Normal] Approved/Prohibited Uses Policy (included in the written plan). Independent Medical Authority Statement (included in the written plan). IT Data Security Checklist (coordinated with campus IT). Target: May 2026.
[Heading 1] Recommendation 4: Selecting & Implementing New Technologies
[Heading 2] What This Means for Baylor
[Normal] No more ad hoc purchasing. Every new technology, whether it is a wearable device, a software platform, a mobile app, or a survey tool, should go through a defined evaluation process before it is purchased and deployed. The NCAA wants this to be a group decision driven by evidence, not a single department acting on vendor marketing.
[Heading 2] Strategy 4.1: Use Evidence-Based Evaluation Standards
[Normal] Key Actions:
[List Paragraph] Develop a Technology Evaluation Checklist that every proposed technology must complete before purchase approval. The checklist should be filled out by the requesting department and reviewed by the Working Group.
[Normal] Draft Template: Technology Evaluation Checklist
[Normal] Scoring: 1 = Does not meet criteria, 5 = Fully meets criteria. A technology should score at a minimum of 3 on every criterion and achieve an average of 3.5 or above to proceed. Any score of 1 on Data Security or Student-Athlete Impact is an automatic rejection.
[Normal] Deliverable:
[Normal] Technology Evaluation Checklist Template (1-page form + scoring rubric). Target: May 2026.
[Heading 2] Strategy 4.2: Assess Quality Before Committing
[Normal] Key Actions:
[List Paragraph] Require a pilot/trial period before full purchase whenever possible. Negotiate with vendors for a 30–60-day trial with a single sport or team before committing to a department-wide purchase. During the pilot, collect structured user feedback.
[List Paragraph] Request validation data from vendors. Ask for independent (non-vendor-funded) research demonstrating accuracy and reliability. If no independent research exists, that is a red flag worth noting on the evaluation checklist.
[List Paragraph] Check with peer institutions. Before purchasing, reach out to at least two comparable programs (Big 12 or Power conference) to ask about their experience with the technology. Document the feedback.
[List Paragraph] Conduct a post-implementation review. 90 days after deploying a new technology, the requesting department should report back to the Working Group on: whether the technology is performing as expected, user satisfaction, any issues encountered, and whether it should continue.
[Normal] Draft Template: Pilot Evaluation Report
[Heading 2] Strategy 4.3: Multidisciplinary Purchase Decisions
[Normal] Key Actions:
[List Paragraph] Route all new technology purchase requests through the Working Group. No performance technology should be purchased without Working Group review and approval. This includes free tools, trial conversions, and platforms offered through sponsorship deals.
[List Paragraph] Establish a standard purchase request process:
[List Paragraph] Step 1: Requesting department completes the Technology Evaluation Checklist.
[List Paragraph] Step 2: IT reviews the data security section and provides written clearance or flags concerns.
[List Paragraph] Step 3: Sports medicine reviews student-athlete health/safety implications.
[List Paragraph] Step 4: Legal/compliance reviews vendor contract terms, data ownership, and regulatory considerations.
[List Paragraph] Step 5: Working Group reviews full package and votes to approve, request a pilot, or deny.
[List Paragraph] Step 6: If approved, finance/administration handles procurement. If a pilot is requested, see the pilot process above.
[List Paragraph] Document every decision. Maintain a log of all technology requests, evaluation scores, decisions, and rationale. This creates an audit trail and supports future decision-making.
[Normal] Deliverable:
[Normal] Technology Purchase Request Process (flowchart + written procedure). Purchase Decision Log (spreadsheet). Target: May 2026.
[Heading 1] Recommendation 5: Continuous Improvement
[Heading 2] What This Means for Baylor
[Normal] The written plan is a living document. The NCAA expects us to actively monitor how technologies are being used, whether they are delivering value, and, most importantly, whether student-athletes are experiencing any negative effects. Student-athlete feedback is not a nice-to-have; the NCAA calls it "critical." We need structured mechanisms to collect, interpret, and act on feedback from all stakeholders.
[Heading 2] Strategy 5.1: Multidisciplinary Feedback Collection
[Normal] Key Actions:
[List Paragraph] Task the Working Group with leading the annual feedback cycle. The same group that developed the plan should be evaluating its effectiveness. This ensures continuity and accountability.
[List Paragraph] Schedule an Annual Performance Technology Review Meeting (separate from regular Working Group meetings). This dedicated session should:
[List Paragraph] Review all feedback collected during the year (surveys, focus groups, incident reports).
[List Paragraph] Evaluate each technology against its stated purpose: is it delivering the expected value?
[List Paragraph] Identify any policy gaps, compliance issues, or areas where the plan needs updating.
[List Paragraph] Set priorities for the coming year (new trainings needed, technologies to add or remove, policy revisions).
[List Paragraph] Document decisions and updates in the plan revision log.
[List Paragraph] Produce an Annual Performance Technology Report (2-3 pages) summarizing findings and actions taken. Share with athletics administration.
[Normal] Deliverable:
[Normal] Annual Performance Technology Review Meeting Agenda Template and Annual Report Template. Target: First cycle completes Spring 2027.
[Normal] Draft Template: Annual Review Meeting Agenda
[Heading 2] Strategy 5.2: Prioritize Student-Athlete Feedback
[Normal] Student-athlete feedback is the most important input in the continuous improvement process. The NCAA uses the word "critical" deliberately. We need a structured way to hear from student-athletes that goes beyond assuming they are fine because they have not complained.
[Normal] Key Actions:
[List Paragraph] Develop an annual student-athlete survey. Administer once per year (recommended: end of spring semester) to capture the full year’s experience. Keep it short (10-15 questions) to maximize response rates.
[Normal] Draft Template: Draft Student-Athlete Performance Technology Survey
[List Paragraph] Supplement surveys with qualitative feedback. Consider one or two annual focus group sessions with student-athletes from different sports. SAAC meetings can also serve as a forum for surfacing concerns. Qualitative feedback captures nuance that Likert scales miss.
[List Paragraph] Establish a confidential concern reporting channel. Student-athletes should have a way to raise concerns outside of surveys. This could be a dedicated email address, an anonymous online form, or a designated point of contact (e.g., the Data Steward or a member of the Student-Athlete Advisory Committee).
[List Paragraph] Share results with student-athletes. Close the feedback loop. Share a brief summary of survey findings and any actions taken at a SAAC meeting or through team communication. This builds trust and encourages future participation.
[Normal] Deliverable:
[Normal] Annual Student-Athlete Survey (digital, administered via survey platform). Confidential Concern Reporting Channel (email or anonymous form). Target: Survey launches Spring 2027; reporting channel established Fall 2026.
[Heading 2] Strategy 5.3: Evaluate Implementation and Effectiveness
[Normal] Key Actions:
[List Paragraph] Develop a Staff Feedback Survey (brief, annual). Administer to all staff involved with performance technologies.
[Normal] Draft Template: Draft Staff Performance Technology Survey
[List Paragraph] Conduct a technology-by-technology effectiveness review. For each technology in use, the Working Group should evaluate annually:
[List Paragraph] Implementation: Are we using it the way we intended? Are all staff following protocols?
[List Paragraph] Effectiveness: Are the outcomes matching the reasons we adopted it? Is it delivering measurable value?
[List Paragraph] Student-athlete impact: Is it causing any reported negative effects?
[List Paragraph] Cost: Is the ongoing cost justified by the value delivered?
[List Paragraph] Decision: Continue as-is / Modify usage / Discontinue.
[List Paragraph] Evaluate education effectiveness. Use training attendance records, survey feedback (both SA and staff), and observed knowledge gaps to determine whether education programs are landing. Update curriculum as needed.
[Normal] Deliverable:
[Normal] Annual Staff Survey, Technology Effectiveness Review Template, and Education Effectiveness Assessment. All part of the annual review cycle beginning Spring 2027.
[Heading 1] Master Implementation Timeline
[Normal] The following consolidates all five recommendations into a single timeline. The approach builds the foundation quickly, leverages existing structures, and targets full implementation by the start of the 2026-27 academic year, with the first complete feedback cycle closing in Spring 2027.
[Heading 2] Summary of Key Deliverables
[Heading 2] Closing
[Normal] This plan is designed to be thorough but practical. We are leveraging existing structures wherever we can (annual compliance sessions, SAAC, campus IT, and legal), so this does not become an unsustainable burden on top of everything else the department is managing. The Working Group is the engine that keeps all of this moving, which is why standing it up first is the immediate priority.
[Normal] This is a working document. It will get better with input from the people in the room. I am ready to start pulling the group together as soon as you give the green light.
--TABLE--
What the NCAA Says:
It is recommended that schools establish a written plan that addresses the responsible use of performance technologies. Having a written plan can help establish common standards and procedures, increase transparency, and address school-specific needs and resources.
--TABLE--
NCAA Strategy: Engage a multidisciplinary team in developing, routinely reviewing, and revising a written plan, leveraging existing campus resources and systems. Key roles on that team may include, but are not limited to, student-athletes, sports medicine staff, coaches, athletics administration, legal affairs, and information technology.
--TABLE--
Section | Content
Purpose | Establish and maintain Baylor Athletics' written plan for the responsible use of performance technologies in alignment with NCAA Sport Science Institute recommendations.
Membership | Chair: [TBD] Student-Athletes: [Names, Sports] Sports Medicine: [Name, Title] S&C: [Name, Title] Coaching: [Name, Sport] and [Name, Sport] Administration: [Name, Title] Legal/Compliance: [Name, Title] IT: [Name, Title]
Meeting Cadence | Monthly (March-June 2026), Quarterly (July 2026 onward)
Responsibilities | 1. Develop written plan 2. Review/approve new technology purchases 3. Oversee education programs 4. Collect and act on feedback 5. Ensure legal/regulatory compliance
Decision Process | Consensus-based; Chair breaks ties. Legal holds veto on compliance matters.
Reporting | Chair reports to [AD/Senior Administrator] after each meeting.
Review | Charter reviewed annually at the first meeting of each academic year.
--TABLE--
NCAA Strategy: Address school-specific considerations, including how relevant groups will be educated, how data will be managed, how decisions will be made about selecting and implementing new technologies and how continuous improvement will be approached.
--TABLE--
Plan Section | Content to Address | Owner
1. Purpose & Scope | Why the plan exists, what it covers, which technologies and personnel fall under it | Chair
2. Definitions | Performance technology, biometric data, performance data, informed consent, data steward, etc. | Chair + Legal
3. Roles & Responsibilities | Who does what: Working Group, coaches, S&C, sports medicine, IT, student-athletes, administration | Chair
4. Student-Athlete Rights | Informed consent process, right to decline, data access rights, grievance process | Legal
5. Data Governance | Data ownership, storage, access controls, retention, transfer protocol, breach response (see Rec 3) | IT + Legal
6. Technology Evaluation | Criteria and process for vetting new technologies before purchase (see Rec 4) | S&C + Sports Med
7. Education Requirements | Who gets trained, how often, on what topics, and how completion is tracked (see Rec 2) | Chair
8. Continuous Improvement | Feedback mechanisms, annual review process, plan revision protocol (see Rec 5) | Chair
9. Compliance | Applicable laws (FERPA, state privacy, biometric), NCAA guidance references, institutional policies | Legal + Compliance
10. Appendices | Consent form template, tech evaluation checklist, education curriculum outlines, feedback survey | Various
--TABLE--
Milestone | Description | Target Date
Working Group Formed | Chair identified, members recruited, charter signed | March 2026
First Meeting | Review the NCAA document, assign plan sections to owners | Early April 2026
Section Drafts Due | Each owner submits their section draft to the chair | Late April 2026
Full Draft Assembled | Chair compiles all sections into a unified document | Early May 2026
Legal/Compliance Review | Legal reviews full draft, provides redlines | Mid-May 2026
Working Group Final Review | Group reviews legal feedback, makes final edits | Late May 2026
Plan Approved | Chair and AD sign off; plan distributed to department | June 2026
First Annual Review | Working group reviews and updates the plan | August/September 2026
--TABLE--
What the NCAA Says:
It is recommended that schools routinely provide education about the responsible use of performance technologies to those involved with their use. Education is foundational for informed consent, and it aids in ensuring schools use performance technologies in a way that maximizes benefits and minimizes harm to student-athletes.
--TABLE--
NCAA Strategy: At least once annually, provide education to those involved in selecting, using or accessing data from performance technologies.
--TABLE--
Audience | Session | Timing | Duration | Delivery | Tracked?
All Staff | Annual Compliance Meeting | August (preseason) | 30-45 min | In-person | Sign-in sheet
New Student-Athletes | Orientation | August/January | 20-30 min | In-person | Sign-in sheet
Returning SAs | Preseason Meeting | August | 10-15 min | In-person | Sign-in sheet
New Hires | Onboarding | Within 30 days of hire | 30 min | 1-on-1 or small group | HR checklist
Working Group | Annual Review Meeting | September | 60-90 min | In-person | Meeting minutes
--TABLE--
NCAA Strategy: Educational needs are likely to vary among different groups and schools should consider tailoring education to meet each group's learning needs. Such groups may include, but are not limited to, student-athletes, coaches, strength and conditioning staff, sports medicine staff and administration.
--TABLE--
Topic | Key Message
What We Collect | We use [GPS trackers/heart rate monitors/body comp tools/wellness surveys/etc.] to help us keep you healthy and help you perform your best. Here is specifically what each tool measures.
Who Sees It | Your data is shared only with [specific roles]. Coaches can see [specific data types]. They cannot see [restricted data types]. Sports medicine has access to health-related data to make medical decisions.
Your Rights | You have the right to know what is collected, ask questions, and decline participation without penalty. If you consent, you can withdraw at any time.
Data After You Leave | When you graduate, your data is [retained for X years/deleted within X days]. If you transfer, [transfer protocol summary].
If Something Feels Wrong | If you feel stressed about your data, if someone is using it in a way that feels inappropriate, or if you have any questions, talk to [contact person/title]. You can also raise concerns through [SAAC/anonymous reporting process].
--TABLE--
Audience | Primary Focus Areas | Estimated Length
Student-Athletes | Rights, consent, data use, mental health, how to raise concerns | 20-30 min
Coaches | Responsible use, data access boundaries, limitations, independent medical authority | 30 min
S&C Staff | Device operation, data collection protocols, quality control, escalation to sports medicine | 30-45 min
Sports Medicine | Data-informed clinical decisions, independent medical authority, privacy obligations, return-to-play | 30 min
Administration | Policy compliance, risk management, legal obligations, procurement oversight, data security | 30 min
IT | Data storage, encryption, access controls, vendor security review, breach response protocols | 30 min
--TABLE--
NCAA Strategy: Address topics such as: limitations and potential harms of performance technologies; data privacy and security; student-athlete rights and protections (e.g., informed consent); departmental policies and procedures for responsible use.
--TABLE--
Required Topic | What to Cover | Why It Matters
1. Limitations & Potential Harms | No technology is perfectly accurate. Results can be misleading if context is missing. Mental health risks include data fixation, anxiety, body image concerns. Over-reliance on data can undermine coaching instincts and athlete autonomy. | Prevents overconfidence in data and protects student-athlete well-being.
2. Data Privacy & Security | What data is collected, where it is stored, who can access it, how long it is retained, what happens in a breach, and what laws apply (FERPA, state privacy, etc.). | Legal obligation and trust-building with student-athletes.
3. Student-Athlete Rights | Informed consent process, voluntary participation, right to withdraw, right to access own data, right to know how data is used, grievance process. | Foundational to ethical use and NCAA expectations.
4. Departmental Policies | Overview of the written plan, roles and responsibilities, technology evaluation process, feedback mechanisms, consequences for policy violations. | Ensures everyone operates under the same standards.
--TABLE--
What the NCAA Says:
It is recommended that schools establish who owns data from performance technologies, where and how data is stored, who has the authority to access data and how data is permitted to be used. Performance technologies have different use-case scenarios and produce different types of data, and the interpretation and communication of data may benefit from a multidisciplinary approach.
--TABLE--
NCAA Strategy: Determine who can be involved in interpreting and sharing/communicating data from performance technologies, including considerations for the required competencies and oversight necessary to do so effectively and responsibly.
--TABLE--
Technology | Data Produced | Collected By | Interpreted By | Shared With | Stored Where
[e.g., GPS Tracker] | Distance, speed, acceleration, player load | S&C Staff | S&C / Sport Scientist | Coaches (summary), Sports Med (if injury-related) | [Vendor cloud / campus server]
[e.g., Heart Rate Monitor] | HR, HRV, recovery metrics | S&C Staff | S&C / Sports Med | Sports Med (clinical), Coaches (aggregate only) | [Vendor platform]
[e.g., Body Comp Tool] | Body fat %, lean mass, etc. | Sports Med / S&C | Sports Med | Restricted: Sports Med only unless SA consents to share | [Campus server]
[e.g., Wellness Survey] | Sleep, soreness, stress, mood | S&C / Sports Med | Sports Med / Sport Psych | Coaches (flagged concerns only, no raw scores) | [Survey platform]
[Add rows as needed] |  |  |  |  | 
--TABLE--
Data Type | Sports Med | S&C | Coaches | Administration | Student-Athlete
Individual health/medical | Full access | Flagged concerns only | No access | No access | Full access (own data)
Individual training load | Full access | Full access | Summary with context | No access | Full access (own data)
Individual body comp | Full access | With SA consent | No access | No access | Full access (own data)
Wellness survey (raw) | Full access | Flagged concerns only | No access | No access | Full access (own data)
Team aggregates | Full access | Full access | Full access | Summary reports | Team-level only
--TABLE--
NCAA Strategy: Determine what rights, if any, the school has with respect to data collection, data use, data access and ownership of the performance technology data, including considerations for transfer student-athletes.
--TABLE--
Section | Sample Language
Purpose | Baylor Athletics uses performance technologies to support your health, safety, and athletic performance. This form explains what data we collect, how we use it, and your rights regarding that data.
Technologies Used | [List specific technologies used by the student-athlete's sport, e.g., "Catapult GPS units during practice and competition, InBody body composition scans, daily wellness surveys via [platform]."]
Data Collected | The following types of data may be collected: [list specific data types, e.g., heart rate, GPS movement data, body composition measurements, sleep quality, self-reported wellness scores].
How Data Is Used | Your data will be used to: monitor training load and recovery, support injury prevention, inform return-to-play decisions (by sports medicine staff), and evaluate the effectiveness of training programs.
Who Has Access | Your data will be accessible to: [list specific roles and what they can see, consistent with the Data Access Matrix]. Your individual data will not be shared with anyone outside these roles without your written permission.
Your Rights | Participation is voluntary. You may decline to participate or withdraw consent at any time without penalty or impact on your athletic scholarship, playing time, or standing on the team. You have the right to: view your own data, ask questions about how it is used, and request corrections or deletion (subject to legal retention requirements).
Data Retention | Your data will be retained for [X years] after your departure from Baylor Athletics. After this period, data will be securely deleted. You may request earlier deletion upon departure.
Transfer Protocol | If you transfer to another institution, your data will not be sent to the new school without your written request. You may request a copy of your data at any time.
Contact | If you have questions or concerns about your data, contact [Data Steward name, title, email, phone].
Signature | I have read and understand this consent form. I voluntarily agree to participate in performance technology data collection as described above.  Student-Athlete Signature: _____________ Date: _______ Printed Name: _______________
--TABLE--
NCAA Strategy: Clarify the school's permissible uses of data from performance technologies. If data might be used to inform medical decision-making, sports medicine staff should be involved. Schools should refer to independent medical care best practices to ensure the unchallengeable, autonomous authority of primary athletics healthcare providers to determine medical management and return-to-play decisions.
--TABLE--
Approved Uses | Prohibited Uses
Monitoring training load to prevent overtraining | Using data to punish or publicly shame a student-athlete
Supporting injury prevention through workload management | Sharing individual data with media, NIL partners, or agents without written SA consent
Informing return-to-play decisions (sports medicine only) | Using body composition data to restrict access to meals or dining
Evaluating effectiveness of training programs | Making scholarship or roster decisions based solely on technology data
Identifying trends that may indicate injury risk | Allowing coaches to override sports medicine return-to-play decisions based on performance data
Supporting sport science research (with IRB approval and SA consent) | Selling or sharing data with third parties
Providing student-athletes with their own data upon request | Retaining data beyond the stated retention period without legal basis
--TABLE--
What the NCAA Says:
It is recommended that schools establish a structured process for making decisions about selecting and implementing new performance technologies. A structured process that considers how to use performance technologies in a way that maximizes benefits and minimizes harm is important to ensure student-athlete well-being is prioritized.
--TABLE--
NCAA Strategy: Review technologies using existing, evidence-based standards and frameworks that evaluate their value, usability, and quality.
--TABLE--
Evaluation Criteria | Questions to Answer | Score (1-5)
1. Scientific Validity | Is there peer-reviewed research supporting the technology's claims? Has it been validated in collegiate or athletic populations? Are the vendor's claims backed by independent evidence? | [  ]
2. Accuracy | Does the device measure what it claims to measure? What is the margin of error? Has accuracy been tested across different conditions (e.g., different sports, environments)? | [  ]
3. Reliability | Does the device produce consistent results under the same conditions? What is the test-retest reliability? | [  ]
4. Data Security | Where is data stored? Is it encrypted? Who has access? What is the vendor's breach notification policy? Is the vendor compliant with relevant regulations? | [  ]
5. Data Portability | Can data be exported in standard formats? What happens to data if we discontinue the platform? | [  ]
6. Usability | How easy is it to use for staff and student-athletes? What training is required? Is the user interface intuitive? | [  ]
7. Integration | Does it integrate with our existing systems? Are there compatibility issues with other technologies we use? | [  ]
8. Cost-Benefit | What is the total cost (purchase, subscription, maintenance, training)? Does the expected value justify the expense? What is the expected ROI? | [  ]
9. Fit with Program Needs | Does this technology solve an actual problem we have? Or is it a solution looking for a problem? Is there a cheaper or simpler alternative? | [  ]
10. Student-Athlete Impact | Could this technology have unintended negative effects on student-athlete well-being? Does it require significant time or effort from student-athletes? | [  ]
--TABLE--
NCAA Strategy: Consider and assess the quality of performance technologies. Quality may include, but is not limited to, factors such as accuracy, reliability, validity, and function.
--TABLE--
Section | Content
Technology Name | [Name, vendor, version]
Pilot Duration | [Start date] to [End date]
Sport/Team | [Sport used during pilot]
Requesting Department | [S&C / Sports Med / Coaching / etc.]
Purpose | Why we are evaluating this technology and what problem it is intended to solve.
Evaluation Checklist Score | [Overall score from the Technology Evaluation Checklist]
Pilot Findings | Did the technology perform as claimed? Were there accuracy or reliability issues? How did staff and student-athletes respond?
User Feedback Summary | What did staff say? What did student-athletes say?
Issues Encountered | Any technical problems, data security concerns, integration challenges, or negative student-athlete feedback?
Recommendation | Approve for full purchase / Extend pilot / Do not purchase. Rationale:
Submitted By | [Name, Title, Date]
--TABLE--
NCAA Strategy: Decisions about selecting and implementing performance technologies should be made by a multidisciplinary group. Important roles to consider include sports medicine staff and individuals with competencies in sports science, coaching staff, information technology, data security, administration, and compliance.
--TABLE--
What the NCAA Says:
It is recommended that schools routinely get feedback from those using performance technologies about how these technologies are being used and how they are working. This feedback can be used to inform changes to the school's written plan to reflect current needs, available resources and evolving technological developments.
--TABLE--
NCAA Strategy: Engage a multidisciplinary group to plan, collect, and interpret feedback about performance technologies. When possible, this group should include individuals involved in establishing the school's written plan for responsible use.
--TABLE--
Agenda Item | Led By | Time
1. Review of feedback: student-athlete survey results | Chair / Student-Athlete Reps | 20 min
2. Review of feedback: staff survey results/observations | Chair | 15 min
3. Technology-by-technology effectiveness review | S&C / Sports Med | 20 min
4. Education program assessment: Did training meet needs? | Chair | 10 min
5. Policy compliance review: any incidents or gaps? | Legal / Compliance | 10 min
6. Proposed plan updates for the coming year | All | 15 min
7. Action items and next steps | Chair | 10 min
--TABLE--
NCAA Strategy: Understanding student-athletes' experiences with performance technology is critical. Schools should obtain student-athlete feedback to learn about the positive and/or negative impacts performance technology use has on their student-athletes.
--TABLE--

1 | I understand what performance technology data is collected about me. | Strongly Disagree to Strongly Agree (1-5)

NCAA Strategy: Areas for feedback from additional groups could include: technology implementation (e.g., how were technologies used), technology effectiveness (e.g., how did outcomes align with the school's reasons for their use), and education (e.g., does education meet learner needs).

Title: NCAA SSI Webinar — Performance Tech & Data Governance
DateString: 2026-09-09T16:01:39.247Z
Duration: 45.290000915527344
Organizer Email: eric.rash11@gmail.com
Meeting Link: No meeting link
Summary: Short Summary: Responsible performance technology in collegiate athletics requires balancing innovation with student-athlete health, safety, and mental well-being. Recommendations emphasized thoughtful policies, education, secure data management, athlete consent, stakeholder feedback, and regular review. Wearables, equipment sensors, optical systems, lab-grade tools, and personal surveys can measure physical and subjective factors, but they must support—not replace—context-aware judgment. Written plans should address validity, reliability, ownership, access, usage, and unintended consequences. Legal, IT, and risk-management review is important because privacy laws vary, data may be sensitive, de-identification can fail, and vendors may resell or reuse information. Staff and coaches need training, while athletes should understand collection practices and participation rights. No single metric reliably predicts performance or risk, and opaque algorithms can undermine trust. Integrating medical and performance data may support injury-risk analysis, but technology should be retained only when it produces actionable value through multidisciplinary collaboration and ongoing learning., Keywords: performance technology, student athlete data, data privacy, educational programs, injury prevention, policy development, Action Items: 
**Tim Coffey**
Engage with student athletes to gather feedback on their experiences and perceptions regarding performance technologies and data use (38:18)
Encourage continuous education of performance and sports medicine staff on validity, reliability, and interpretation of performance technology data (21:46)

**Mark Koberly**
Develop and maintain a written plan/policy framework for performance technology adoption including justification, validity checks, data privacy, and access protocols (13:37)
Coordinate with institutional general counsel, IT, and risk management to ascertain legal and security compliance in data collection, storage, and use (31:06)
Implement routine reevaluations of performance technology effectiveness based on actionable outcomes and stakeholder feedback (17:22)

**Tim Coffey and Mark Koberly**
Promote multidisciplinary stakeholder education including coaches and student athletes before deploying new technology (21:46)
Advocate for transparency and consent regarding data collection and use with student athletes to mitigate anxiety and privacy concerns (20:16)

[3] Id: 01M20RY1448X3AG6HN25DCER8K
Title: Acro & Tumbling — Impact Load Tracking Pilot
DateString: 2026-09-08T15:07:08.895Z
Duration: 26.75
Organizer Email: eric.rash11@gmail.com
Meeting Link: No meeting link
Summary: Short Summary: The team discussed building a simple system to measure tumbling workload by assigning fixed impact counts to individual skills and summing them through a routine builder or digital spreadsheet. The purpose is to improve objective workload visibility, balance strength and tumbling volume, and avoid excessive volume spikes—not specifically to prevent injuries. Because athletes may take different numbers of attempts, change assignments, or perform extra repetitions, tracking must record actual work rather than only planned passes. The pilot will include no more than five tumblers, mixing reliable and less consistent reporters, and will initially focus on core competition skills while excluding non-floor impacts such as trampoline drills. A standardized skill inventory with consistent names and impact counts will serve as the source of truth. Manual logging on paper, a whiteboard, or Excel is the practical starting point, supported by athlete self-reporting after practice. The team also noted open-gym work, limited staffing, and changing practice schedules as challenges, while identifying wearable or force-sensor technology as a future option., Keywords: Tumbling, Impact Counting, Routine Builder, Practice Load, Pilot Group, Skill Inventory, Action Items: 
**Unassigned**
Compile and send an inventory list of all tumbling skills with the associated hand/foot impact counts for each skill (15:42)
Provide daily tumbling assignments or passes planned for practices to support data logging (15:42)
Select and manage a pilot group (around five tumblers) responsible for tracking their tumbling reps and impacts each practice (09:00)
Create a consistent naming convention for tumbling skills to ensure tracking and data aggregation accuracy (21:30)

**Eric Rash**
Develop an Excel-based “pass builder” tool for mapping tumbling routines and calculating cumulative impact loads from skill counts (01:35)
Support integrating daily data from practice assignments into the tool once the inventory and assignments are provided (15:42)
